c.tagline: Mediterranean capital where Roman ruins meet Ottoman souks.

taxi.fareNote: Meters exist but are rarely used in practice; agree on the fare with the driver before setting off, especially from the airport or as a foreign visitor.

emergency.note: Emergency response can be inconsistent given the ongoing political and security instability; hotels and tour fixers are often the fastest way to get help.

avoid.reason: Most governments advise against all travel to Libya; in Tripoli avoid the southern districts and outskirts where militia clashes flare (e.g. Abu Salim and around checkpoints), and leave any area with armed gatherings immediately.
Kidnapping, carjacking and sudden armed clashes are real risks anywhere; never photograph checkpoints, keep a low profile, and move only with trusted local contacts.

hood_desc: Tripoli's walled Ottoman/Ottoman-Karamanli-era old town of souks, mosques, and the Red Castle museum; atmospheric for day exploring but has almost no formal lodging of its own, so most visitors base themselves nearby.

The city's political and commercial heart on the Mediterranean corniche around Martyrs' (Green) Square, home to Tripoli's flagship international-standard hotels, ministries, and main shopping streets; the default base for business travelers and anyone wanting central, more secure lodging.
A sprawling western coastal strip of restaurants, supermarkets, and diplomatic residences favored by expatriates, oil-sector staff, and NGO workers; convenient for longer stays but car-dependent.
An upscale, leafy residential district just west of downtown popular with diplomats and wealthier Tripolitans, with quieter streets and some of the city's newer high-rise developments.
A quieter western coastal suburb near the Tripoli Golf Club, appealing to longer-term visitors and those wanting a resort-style base away from the downtown core.

water.note: Tap water is not recommended for visitors; use bottled or treated water.

transit.pay: Cash only, paid directly to the driver or conductor in Libyan dinars; there is no unified fare card, app, or digital payment system.
transit.hours: Buses generally run early morning to early evening with sparse frequency; little to no service after dark, when private or shared taxis are the norm.
transit.note: Public transit is informal, aimed at residents rather than tourists, and route information is not published online; most visitors rely on hotel transfers or pre-arranged drivers.

bus: Intercity buses connecting Tripoli to Benghazi, Misrata, Sabha, and other Libyan cities

airport.name: Mitiga International Airport (MJI)
airport.drive: 15-25 min from downtown, depending on traffic and checkpoints

transit.m: Hotel/pre-arranged private transfer (no scheduled public transit to the airport)

tip.r: Not culturally obligatory; rounding up or a small tip (5-10%) is appreciated in restaurants and hotels catering to foreign visitors.
